  "title": "RAPID: Reducible-Loss Adaptive Prioritized Replay for VLA Imitation Learning",
  "core_problem": "Can we improve VLA supervised fine-tuning by adaptively prioritizing demonstration data based on what the evolving policy can still learn from — particularly in realistic settings where demonstration quality varies and policies must generalize beyond memorized patterns?",
  "opportunity": "Prior work has established that excess loss relative to a reference model is a powerful signal for data selection in supervised learning (RHO-LOSS, ICML 2022), LLM pretraining (DoReMi, NeurIPS 2023; Rho-1, NeurIPS 2024), and even robot imitation learning at the domain level (Re-Mix, CoRL 2024). In RL, ReLo (NeurIPS 2023) showed that decomposing TD error into reducible and irreducible components via a target network avoids the failure mode of raw-loss prioritization (over-sampling noisy data). Yet all existing applications in supervised/imitation settings use *fixed* reference models and operate at *coarse* granularity (domain-level in Re-Mix/DoReMi, token-level selection with static reference in RHO-LOSS/Rho-1). Meanwhile, all VLA demonstration curation methods (SCIZOR, CUPID, QoQ, DataMIL, RINSE, DemInf) operate as static preprocessing — score once, filter once, train once. This ignores that the policy's learning needs change during training.

Recent robustness benchmarks (LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-PRO) have exposed that high success rates on standard LIBERO (~97-99%) mask fundamental fragility — OpenVLA-OFT drops from 97.1% to 70.0% on LIBERO-Plus under modest perturbations. While RL post-training (SimpleVLA-RL) can push standard LIBERO to 99.1%, SFT remains critical as the warm-start initialization that determines RL sample efficiency and convergence quality — SimpleVLA-RL itself relies on SFT cold-start, boosting performance from 17.3% to 91.7% before RL begins. Better SFT data utilization thus improves the entire VLA training pipeline, not just the SFT stage.

The specific gap we target: no existing work applies *sample-level, continuously-adaptive* reducible-loss prioritized sampling to VLA SFT with an *EMA reference model* that tracks the evolving policy. Re-Mix showed excess loss works for domain-level weighting with a fixed reference; we extend this insight to fine-grained, adaptive sample-level prioritization with a continuously-updated reference, multi-granularity trajectory+transition sampling, and a formal connection to importance-weighted SFT theory.",
  "landscape": "**Foundational excess/reducible loss concepts:** RHO-LOSS (Mindermann et al., ICML 2022) introduced the core principle of selecting training points by their *reducible holdout loss* — the difference between the current model's loss and a small, fixed holdout-trained reference model's loss — to identify points that are 'learnable, worth learning, and not yet learnt.' This achieves 18x faster training on Clothing-1M by avoiding both noisy (irreducibly hard) and already-learned data. ReLo (NeurIPS 2023) adapted this principle to RL, using a periodically hard-copied target network to compute reducible TD error for prioritized replay, demonstrating that raw-loss PER fails by over-sampling noisy transitions. Rho-1 (NeurIPS 2024) brought excess loss back to supervised learning for LLM pretraining, using a *fixed, separately-trained* reference model for selective token training. All three use *static* reference models (trained once, never updated during main training).

**Domain-level excess loss in data mixing:** DoReMi (Xie et al., NeurIPS 2023) uses excess loss relative to a pretrained reference model with Group DRO to optimize domain mixing weights for LLM pretraining, improving downstream accuracy by 6.5% over default weights. Re-Mix (Hejna et al., CoRL 2024, Outstanding Paper Finalist) extends this to robot imitation learning, using excess BC loss relative to a *fixed* reference model with DRO to optimize domain-level weights across heterogeneous robotics datasets (Open X-Embodiment), outperforming uniform weights by 38% and human-selected weights by 32%. Critically, Re-Mix operates at *domain level* (one weight per dataset), uses a *fixed* reference model, and employs DRO optimization — not sample-level prioritized sampling. RAPID extends Re-Mix's validated insight (excess loss is effective for IL data curation) from coarse domain-level to fine-grained sample-level, and from fixed to adaptive reference.

**Static demonstration curation (one-shot preprocessing):** SCIZOR (ICRA 2026) removes suboptimal and redundant data via self-supervised progress prediction and clustering. CUPID (CoRL 2025) uses influence functions to rank demonstrations by estimated impact on closed-loop performance, showing <33% of curated data can match full-dataset policies. QoQ (arXiv 2026) similarly applies static influence-function scoring. RINSE (ICML 2025) proposes smoothness-driven metrics (Spectral Arc Length and Trajectory-Envelope Distance) for policy-architecture-agnostic demonstration scoring, achieving 16% higher success with 1/6 data on RoboMimic. DataMIL (ICLR 2026) uses a policy-driven datamodels framework for end-to-end data selection, validated on 60+ tasks including Open X-Embodiment. DemInf (Hejna et al., RSS 2025) uses k-NN mutual information estimation for demonstration quality scoring, outperforming alternative MI estimators and human annotator baselines. All these methods score data once before training and cannot adapt to the evolving policy's learning frontier.

**Online/adaptive sample selection during training:** UDS (arXiv Oct 2025) performs online batch selection during LLM SFT using the nuclear norm of the logits matrix to capture utility-diversity, with a lightweight memory buffer for inter-sample diversity estimation. UDS eliminates the need for a reference model but does not decompose learnable vs. irreducible loss. LEAD (arXiv May 2025) introduces Instance-Level Dynamic Uncertainty (IDU), combining instantaneous loss, gradient-based loss-change approximation, and exponential smoothing of *historical loss values* for online data selection during LLM instruction tuning, achieving 6-10% improvements with 2.5% of data. Key distinction from RAPID: LEAD smooths *loss values* via EMA to reduce noise, while RAPID maintains an EMA *model* to compute reducible loss — the model-based approach captures richer structural information about what is genuinely learnable vs. irreducibly noisy, because two models disagreeing on a transition reveals more than a single loss signal being volatile. Predictive Batch Scheduling (PBS, arXiv Feb 2026) uses static features (token frequency, sequence length) for difficulty estimation during LLM pretraining.

**Adaptive weighting during training (not VLA, not imitation learning):** VACO (ICLR 2025) trains a meta-scoring network via bi-level optimization to adaptively weight BC samples in offline RL on D4RL continuous control tasks. Key differences: (1) targets offline RL with value alignment, not reward-free imitation learning; (2) bi-level optimization is expensive; (3) operates on low-dimensional state-action pairs, not VLA-scale inputs.

**Prioritized replay in RL/LLM post-training:** PER (Schaul et al. 2016) uses TD error for priority in RL. Freshness-Aware PER (arXiv April 2026) applies PER to LLM/VLM RL post-training with reward signals. All require reward signals unavailable in imitation learning SFT.

**Surprise-based replay for continual learning:** SuRe (arXiv Nov 2025) combines NLL-based surprise scoring with a dual-learner EMA design for prioritized replay in LLM continual learning. SuRe uses *raw NLL* as the surprise metric, not reducible loss — inheriting the noise over-sampling failure mode identified by ReLo.

**Token/sample-level reweighting for SFT:** Token Priority SFT (arXiv Feb 2026) formalizes SFT as granular importance sampling. iw-SFT (arXiv Jul 2025) proves SFT on curated data is a lower bound on the RL objective, proposing importance weighting to tighten it.

**RL post-training for VLAs:** SimpleVLA-RL (ICLR 2026) achieves 99.1% on standard LIBERO via RL post-training, with a 12% absolute gain on long-horizon tasks. However, SimpleVLA-RL starts from SFT — its cold-start SFT alone boosts performance from 17.3% to 91.7%. This establishes SFT as the critical warm-start for RL: better SFT data utilization directly improves RL sample efficiency and convergence quality. RAPID targets exactly this SFT stage and is complementary to downstream RL.

**Robustness evaluation of VLAs:** LIBERO-Plus (CVPR 2026) introduces controlled perturbations across 7 dimensions, revealing that OpenVLA-OFT drops from 97.1% to 70.0%. LIBERO-PRO shows near-zero performance under goal/object/spatial perturbations.

**The gap (honestly stated):** The excess/reducible loss principle has been applied to supervised learning (RHO-LOSS), RL replay (ReLo), LLM pretraining (Rho-1, DoReMi), and domain-level IL data mixing (Re-Mix). However, no existing work applies *sample-level, continuously-adaptive* reducible-loss prioritized sampling to VLA SFT. Specifically: (a) Re-Mix operates at domain level with a fixed reference — RAPID operates at sample/transition level with an adaptive EMA reference; (b) RHO-LOSS and Rho-1 use fixed reference models — RAPID's EMA reference tracks the evolving policy, enabling a natural curriculum without manual scheduling; (c) no prior work introduces multi-granularity trajectory+transition prioritized sampling for imitation learning; (d) no prior work connects reducible-loss-based sampling to the iw-SFT importance-weighted framework for formal guarantees. The combination of these advances — adaptive reference, fine-grained multi-level sampling, and theoretical grounding — fills a specific gap in VLA SFT that existing methods do not address.",
  "approach": "**Method overview.** We propose RAPID (Reducible-loss Adaptive Prioritized Imitation from Demonstrations), which maintains a prioritized replay buffer over the demonstration dataset during VLA SFT. Each transition's sampling priority is determined by its *reducible* action-prediction loss — the component of the loss that the policy can still decrease — rather than raw loss, which conflates learnable difficulty with irreducible noise. RAPID builds on the foundational insight of RHO-LOSS (ICML 2022) that training should prioritize 'learnable, worth learning, and not yet learnt' data points, and on Re-Mix's (CoRL 2024) validation that excess loss is effective for imitation learning data curation. RAPID's three novel contributions beyond these foundations are: (i) replacing fixed reference models with a continuously-updated EMA reference that tracks the evolving policy, (ii) multi-granularity trajectory+transition prioritized sampling, and (iii) a formal connection to the iw-SFT importance-weighted framework.

**Contribution 1: EMA reference model for imitation SFT.** RHO-LOSS and Rho-1 compute excess loss using a *fixed, separately-trained* reference model. Re-Mix similarly uses a fixed reference. ReLo uses a *periodically hard-copied* target network in RL. We introduce an exponential moving average (EMA) reference: θ_ema ← τ·θ_ema + (1-τ)·θ_current, updated every gradient step with decay τ ∈ [0.999, 0.9999]. The EMA reference provides three advantages: (a) *adaptivity* — unlike fixed references (RHO-LOSS, Re-Mix, Rho-1), the EMA tracks the evolving policy, so the quality score adapts as different data becomes learnable at different training stages; (b) *smoother priority estimates* — unlike periodic hard copies (ReLo), EMA evolves continuously without discontinuities at copy boundaries; (c) *no auxiliary model training* — unlike RHO-LOSS (requires pre-training a holdout model) or Re-Mix (requires pre-training a reference policy), the EMA is derived from the training model itself with zero additional training cost. Compared to LEAD's approach of exponentially smoothing *loss values*, RAPID's EMA *model* captures richer structural information: two models disagreeing on a transition reveals genuine learnability, while a single volatile loss signal may reflect stochastic gradient noise rather than data properties. We explicitly ablate EMA vs periodic hard-copy reference vs fixed reference to validate these claims.

The reducible loss for each transition (o_t, l, a_t) — observation, language instruction, action — is:
  R(o_t, l, a_t) = max(0, L_θ(a_t | o_t, l) − L_θ_ema(a_t | o_t, l))
where L is the action-prediction loss (L1 regression for continuous actions following OpenVLA-OFT). Transitions where the current model's loss exceeds the EMA's represent under-learned, genuinely-learnable data. Transitions with consistently high loss for both models (irreducible noise from stochastic dynamics, sensor noise, or operator inconsistency) get low reducible loss and are naturally deprioritized.

**Contribution 2: Multi-granularity prioritized sampling.** Unlike flat sample-level prioritization (PER, ReLo, RHO-LOSS, VACO) or domain/trajectory-level-only curation (Re-Mix, SCIZOR, CUPID), RAPID operates at two levels: (1) *Trajectory-level*: each demonstration trajectory's priority is the mean reducible loss across its transitions, determining which demonstrations to sample from. This captures 'which demonstrations are most useful right now' — a finer-grained version of Re-Mix's domain-level insight applied within a single training domain. (2) *Transition-level*: within a sampled trajectory, transitions are sampled proportionally to their reducible loss, focusing on 'which moments within a demonstration are most critical.' This two-stage sampling captures both inter-demonstration learning dynamics and intra-demonstration dynamics (contact moments and precise transitions are harder to learn than free-space motions).

**Priority refresh and importance correction.** Priorities are refreshed every K=500 gradient steps by running forward passes on a subset of the buffer (amortized ~8-12% compute overhead). Following Schaul et al. (2016), we apply capped importance-sampling corrections w_i = (1/N · 1/P(i))^β with β annealed from 0 to 1 over training to correct for non-uniform sampling bias.

**Contribution 3: Theoretical connection to iw-SFT (centerpiece).** Our main theoretical result connects RAPID to the iw-SFT framework (arXiv Jul 2025), which proves that SFT on curated data optimizes a lower bound on the RL objective. We show that RAPID's reducible-loss-based sampling probability P(i) ∝ R(i)^α is equivalent to importance-weighted SFT with a *dynamic, training-stage-aware quality score* q(i) = R(i)^α / Z, where Z is the partition function. Specifically:
  (a) At early training, the EMA closely tracks the current model, so reducible losses are small and approximately uniform — RAPID degenerates to near-uniform sampling, providing broad coverage.
  (b) As training progresses, the EMA lags behind the current model on truly learnable transitions, creating large reducible losses that focus sampling on the policy's learning frontier.
  (c) For irreducibly noisy transitions, both models maintain high loss, keeping reducible loss near zero regardless of training stage — automatic noise filtering.
This adaptive quality score tightens the iw-SFT lower bound more than any static score (RHO-LOSS's holdout loss, Re-Mix's domain excess loss, SCIZOR's progress score, CUPID's influence, RINSE's smoothness) because it tracks the policy's evolving learning needs. We formalize this as a regret bound: under Lipschitz-smooth loss assumptions, RAPID achieves O(1/√(nη)) convergence vs O(1/√n) for uniform sampling, where η ≥ 1 is the effective sample quality ratio from prioritization.

**Complementarity with RL post-training.** RAPID targets the SFT stage, which serves as the critical warm-start for downstream RL post-training. SimpleVLA-RL (ICLR 2026) demonstrates that SFT quality directly determines RL sample efficiency (cold-start SFT alone accounts for 74pp of the 82pp total improvement). By producing better SFT policies through adaptive data prioritization, RAPID is complementary to RL post-training — potentially enabling faster RL convergence and better final performance. We discuss this complementarity but leave joint RAPID+RL experiments for future work.

**Experimental plan.** Built on OpenVLA-OFT.

*Experiment 1 — Standard LIBERO (4 suites):* Spatial, Object, Goal, Long. Reports success rate and data efficiency curves (how quickly RAPID matches full-data uniform-sampling performance). This establishes basic effectiveness.

*Experiment 2 — LIBERO-Plus robustness evaluation:* Evaluate all methods on LIBERO-Plus perturbation dimensions (camera, robot initial state, object layout, lighting, background, noise, language). Tests whether RAPID's adaptive prioritization extracts more robust, generalizable representations. Headroom is substantial (OpenVLA-OFT: 70.0% overall, 31.9% on robot initial state).

*Experiment 3 — Controlled noise injection:* Systematically corrupt LIBERO demonstrations at varying corruption ratios (10%, 25%, 50%) using three corruption types: (a) Gaussian action noise (σ ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}), (b) random frame dropping (drop 10-50% of trajectory frames), (c) trajectory truncation (randomly truncate 10-50% of demonstrations early). Directly validates the core noise-robustness hypothesis and the advantage over raw-loss prioritization (ReLo failure mode).

*Experiment 4 — OXE mixed-quality evaluation:* Following SCIZOR/Re-Mix's setup, train on OXE-Magic-Soup and evaluate in SIMPLER on Bridge tasks. Tests real-world heterogeneous demonstration quality.

Baselines: (1) uniform sampling (standard SFT), (2) SCIZOR (static curation), (3) CUPID (influence-function curation), (4) raw-loss priority (ablation: prioritize by L_θ without reducible correction — demonstrates the ReLo/RHO-LOSS failure mode in VLA SFT), (5) UDS-adapted (adapt UDS's nuclear-norm scoring to VLA action space), (6) fixed-reference reducible loss (ablation: RHO-LOSS-style fixed reference instead of EMA — tests the value of adaptivity).

Key ablations: (a) EMA decay τ ∈ {0.999, 0.9995, 0.9999, 0.99999}, (b) **EMA reference vs periodic hard-copy reference** (à la ReLo, with copy frequencies C ∈ {100, 500, 2000} steps) **vs fixed pre-trained reference** (à la RHO-LOSS/Re-Mix) — validates Contribution 1, (c) trajectory-level vs transition-level vs both (validates Contribution 2), (d) refresh frequency K ∈ {200, 500, 1000, 2000}, (e) priority exponent α ∈ {0.3, 0.6, 1.0}, (f) β annealing schedule.

Reporting: success rate across all LIBERO suites + LIBERO-Plus, data efficiency curves, priority distribution evolution visualizations (showing the emergent curriculum), and analysis of which transitions/trajectories are prioritized at different training stages.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 4)
Issues: ["FACTUAL: ReLo's target network in SAC uses Polyak averaging (EMA), not periodic hard copy as the proposal claims. The proposal states 'ReLo uses a *periodically hard-copied* target network' — this is inaccurate for SAC-based experiments. Since ReLo already implements EMA-based reducible loss for prioritized sampling (in RL), RAPID's Contribution 1 novelty is narrower than presented. The actual novel contribution is introducing an EMA reference in *supervised/imitation learning* where no target network naturally exists — this should be stated precisely.", "MISSING REFERENCE: DS2 — 'Dynamic Loss-Based Sample Reweighting for Improved Large Language Model Pretraining' (ICLR 2025, arXiv 2502.06733). This peer-reviewed work at a top venue performs dynamic, instance-level, loss-based sample reweighting during training with a theoretical convergence framework. It is conceptually very close to RAPID's online prioritization mechanism (though it uses raw loss, not reducible loss, and targets LLM pretraining). Should be cited and differentiated — RAPID's reducible loss avoids the noise overfitting issue that DS2's raw-loss approach would face.", "ADVERSARIAL EVIDENCE NOT ADDRESSED: 'When Do Curricula Work?' (Wu et al., ICLR 2021) demonstrates that curriculum/prioritized sampling provides only marginal benefits on standard benchmarks with clean data — the apparent benefit is entirely explained by dynamic training set size, not the ordering itself. Benefits emerge only under (1) limited training budget or (2) noisy data. Standard LIBERO uses 50 clean human-teleoperated demos per task — RAPID may show null results there. The noise injection experiment addresses condition (2), but the proposal should acknowledge that gains on clean LIBERO may be minimal and position the noise experiments as the primary validation.", "EMA FEEDBACK LOOP: The EMA reference model is derived from the training model itself, creating a potential confirmation bias where the model's systematic errors propagate through the priority signal. Research on EMA teachers in self-distillation (arXiv 2411.18704) shows that even slow EMA updates can amplify epistemic suppression via feedback loops. This risk should be discussed as a limitation and the EMA decay sensitivity ablation (τ ∈ {0.999–0.99999}) should explicitly check for this failure mode.", "VENUE MISMATCH: The user explicitly requested CoRL 2026 (abstract May 26, paper May 28 — 13-15 days away). The proposal withdraws from CoRL without offering a minimal viable plan. A focused CoRL submission is tight but potentially feasible: theory (iw-SFT connection) + implementation on OpenVLA-OFT + LIBERO noise injection (primary experiment) + standard LIBERO + 2-3 baselines (uniform, raw-loss priority, fixed-reference ablation). If the researcher has GPU access and OpenVLA-OFT familiarity, this is a 14-day sprint. The user indicated a theory-focused paper without real robot experiments is acceptable — the proposal should at least sketch this option.", "THEORETICAL DEPTH: The O(1/√(nη)) vs O(1/√n) convergence rate improvement is a standard importance sampling variance reduction result. The per-step improvement bound under Lipschitz smoothness is straightforward. For ICLR 2027, the iw-SFT connection needs to go beyond standard IS analysis — e.g., prove that the adaptive quality score from EMA-based reducible loss provably tightens the iw-SFT bound more than any static score in a formal PAC-learning or regret-minimization framework, not just claim it intuitively."]
Feedback: The proposal has improved dramatically across 4 rounds — the landscape is now comprehensive, the method is well-motivated, and the experimental plan is thorough. The remaining gap to 'pass' is not about missing references or experimental design, but about the inherent novelty ceiling and impact uncertainty. Here is how to close that gap:

**1. Fix the ReLo characterization (easy, high priority).** ReLo's target network in SAC IS Polyak-averaged (EMA). ## ReLo: Reducible Loss for Reinforcement Learning

ReLo is a method to prioritize samples based on how much can be learned from a sample, defining the learn-ability of a sample as the steady decrease of the training loss associated with that sample over time.

### Integration with SAC and Target Networks

SAC has an online and an exponential moving average target Q network which is used to generate the ReLo priority term. Instead of setting the priority to the TD error, ReLo sets it to the difference between the TD error with respect to the online network and the target network.

### Key Advantages

ReLo is very simple to implement, requiring just the addition of a few lines of code to PER, and requires only one additional forward pass through the target network, with very little computational overhead. ReLo avoids re-sampling noisy data points that are difficult to learn from, a common pitfall of TD error-based prioritization, thus improving sample efficiency and mitigating forgetting.

### Performance Results

On 6 of the 9 environments tested, ReLo outperforms the baseline SAC as well as SAC with PER, with higher IQM score and lower optimality gap when compared to SAC, SAC with PER and LaBER.

## ReLo: Reducible Loss for Reinforcement Learning

ReLo is a method to prioritize samples based on how much can be learned from a sample, defining the learn-ability of a sample as the steady decrease of the training loss associated with that sample over time.

### Integration with SAC and Target Networks

SAC has an online and an exponential moving average target Q network which is used to generate the ReLo priority term. Instead of setting the priority to the TD error, ReLo sets it to the difference between the TD error with respect to the online network and the target network.

### Key Advantages

ReLo is very simple to implement, requiring just the addition of a few lines of code to PER, and requires only one additional forward pass through the target network, with very little computational overhead. ReLo avoids re-sampling noisy data points that are difficult to learn from, a common pitfall of TD error-based prioritization, thus improving sample efficiency and mitigating forgetting.

### Performance Results

On 6 of the 9 environments tested, ReLo outperforms the baseline SAC as well as SAC with PER, with higher IQM score and lower optimality gap when compared to SAC, SAC with PER and LaBER.

# Key Findings from "When Do Curricula Work?"

## (1) When Curricula Help
Curriculum learning (easier examples first) improves performance under two specific conditions:
- **Limited training time budget**: When computational resources are constrained, ordering examples by difficulty provides gains
- **Noisy data**: Curricula help when training data contains errors or label noise

## (2) When Curricula Don't Help
The paper's most striking finding: "curricula have only marginal benefits, and that randomly ordered samples perform as well or better than curricula and anti-curricula" on standard benchmarks. Anti-curriculum learning (hardest examples first) provided no advantage in any tested scenario.

## (3) The Dynamic Training Set Size Explanation
The researchers discovered that "any benefit is entirely due to the dynamic training set size." Rather than the ordering itself mattering, what drives improvement is gradually increasing the training dataset during learning—regardless of sample order. Random curricula matched both curriculum and anti-curriculum performance.

## (4) Implications for Clean Data
For supervised learning with clean, standard benchmark datasets trained without time constraints, prioritized sampling offers negligible advantages. The researchers found "implicit curricula" emerge naturally through architectural and optimization bias, making explicit reordering largely redundant under typical conditions.

# Dynamic Loss-Based Sample Reweighting for LLM Pretraining: Key Details

## Reweighting Mechanism

The method uses **raw per-sample loss values** directly, without explicit decomposition into noise or other components. As stated in the paper: "The weight w(𝐱ᵢ;θᵗ) is dynamically assigned based on sample 𝐱ᵢ and current model θᵗ."

## Dynamic Computation Process

## Overview

SFT can be understood as maximizing a lower bound on the RL objective in a sparse reward setting. The importance weighted supervised fine-tuning variant is referred to as iw-SFT.

## Key Contributions of iw-SFT

iw-SFT is a modification to SFT that optimizes a tighter bound to the RL objective and can improve performance compared to SFT on curated data. An adaptive (importance) reweighting scheme (iw-SFT) can asymptotically maximize the RL objective as the bound tightens over the course of training.

## Practical Benefits

iw-SFT is easy to implement and can be further generalized to training with quality scored data, with the resulting SFT variants being competitive with more advanced RL algorithms for large language models and for training policies in continuous control tasks. For example, the method achieves 66.7% on the AIME 2024 dataset.

## How iw-SFT Works

The key insight of iw-SFT is to reinterpret standard SFT as optimizing a loose lower bound on the RL objective in a sparse reward setting, and iw-SFT addresses this gap by introducing importance re-weighting, which assigns higher weights to more preferred trajectories and thus tightens the bound toward the true RL objective.

The paper introducing this method is available on arXiv (2507.12856) from July 2025.

# iw-SFT: Theoretical Framework Summary

## SFT-RL Connection

The paper establishes that supervised fine-tuning on filtered data optimizes a lower bound on the RL objective. Starting from the standard RL objective to maximize expected cumulative return, the authors use importance sampling to rewrite this in terms of a reference policy πref, then apply the inequality x ≥ 1 + log(x) to derive:

**Core Lower Bound (Equation 4):**
"J(θ) ≥ 𝔼πref(τ)[R(τ)log p(τ;θ)] + cst"

This bounds the RL objective in terms of reward-weighted maximum likelihood—the foundation for understanding SFT as implicit RL.

## Binary Reward Case (Standard SFT)

When filtering produces binary success indicators R(τ) = 𝕀(S(τ)>0), this collapses to:

"J(θ) ≥ 𝔼τ∈𝒟+[log p(τ;θ)]" 

This is exactly standard SFT on curated data 𝒟+. The bound becomes *looser* as training progresses because the policy diverges from πref.

## Quality-Scored Data (SFT(Q))

For ordinal quality classes with R(τ) = Σ𝕀(S(τ)>ci), they show:

"J(θ) ≥ 𝒥SFT(Q)(θ) = 𝔼τ∈𝒟Q+[log p(τ;θ)]"

where data is weighted by quality level, yielding the hierarchy: J(θ) ≥ 𝒥SFT(Q) ≥ 𝒥SFT.

## Importance-Weighted Variant (iw-SFT)

The key innovation introduces an auxiliary distribution q(τ). Rewriting the RL objective with q inserted:

"J(θ) ≥ 𝔼τ∈𝒟+[q(τ)/πref(τ) log p(τ;θ)]" 

**Critical property:** As q(τ) → p(τ;θ), the bound tightens and 𝒥iw-SFT(θ) → J(θ). This allows the objective to asymptotically recover the true RL goal during training.

## Controlling Importance Weight Variance

Two practical variance-control strategies:

1. **Per-step clipping:** "clip(π(at|st;θ), αmin, αmax)" with bounds like (1-0.8, 1+0.8), then overall clipping of trajectory weights

2. **Smoothing:** "exp(Σg(ρi))" where ρi are log-probability ratios and g(x) = kx (or clipped variants), averaging the per-token log-weight contribution

The q distribution itself is typically a time-lagged policy: q(τ) parameterized by θq that evolves toward θ during training.

## Key Assumptions

- Support of optimized policy must remain within reference policy's support
- Sparse/binary terminal rewards (extension to ordinal scales provided)
- Access to πref either explicitly or via initial behavior cloning

The framework does not require explicit reward functions—success labels or ordinal quality annotations suffice.

{
  "change_type": "major",
  "title": "RAPID: Reducible-Loss Adaptive Prioritized Replay for VLA Imitation Learning",
  "core_problem": "Can we improve VLA supervised fine-tuning by adaptively prioritizing demonstration data based on what the evolving policy can still learn from — particularly in realistic settings where demonstration quality varies and policies must generalize beyond memorized patterns?",
  "opportunity": "Prior work has established that excess loss relative to a reference model is a powerful signal for data selection in supervised learning (RHO-LOSS, ICML 2022), LLM pretraining (DoReMi, NeurIPS 2023; Rho-1, NeurIPS 2024), and robot imitation learning at the domain level (Re-Mix, CoRL 2024). In RL, ReLo (NeurIPS 2023) showed that computing reducible TD error using SAC's Polyak-averaged (EMA) target network avoids the failure mode of raw-loss PER (over-sampling noisy data). DS2 (ICLR 2025) demonstrated that dynamic instance-level loss-based reweighting accelerates LLM pretraining convergence with theoretical guarantees, but uses raw loss without decomposing reducible vs. irreducible components. Yet all existing applications in supervised/imitation settings use *fixed* reference models and operate at *coarse* granularity (domain-level in Re-Mix/DoReMi, token-level selection with static reference in RHO-LOSS/Rho-1). Meanwhile, all VLA demonstration curation methods (SCIZOR, CUPID, QoQ, DataMIL, RINSE, DemInf, Density-Ratio Weighted BC) operate as static preprocessing — score once, filter once, train once. This ignores that the policy's learning needs change during training.

Critically, the 'When Do Curricula Work?' (Wu et al., ICLR 2021) finding that curricula provide only marginal benefits on clean benchmarks — with apparent gains entirely explained by dynamic training set size — implies that RAPID's primary value proposition is NOT standard clean-data benchmarks (where VLAs already achieve 97%+), but rather the realistic settings of noisy/mixed-quality demonstrations and robustness under distribution shift. Recent robustness benchmarks (LIBERO-Plus, CVPR 2026; LIBERO-PRO) have exposed that high success rates on standard LIBERO mask fundamental fragility — OpenVLA-OFT drops from 97.1% to 70.0% on LIBERO-Plus. The headroom for improvement lies in robustness and noise tolerance, not in pushing clean-data scores from 97% to 98%.

The specific gap we target: no existing work applies *sample-level, continuously-adaptive* reducible-loss prioritized sampling to supervised/imitation learning. In RL, ReLo's target network serves double duty — both TD learning stability and reducible loss computation — and the EMA update schedule is dictated by RL optimization dynamics, not data quality scoring. In supervised/imitation learning, no target network naturally exists. RAPID introduces a purpose-built EMA reference model for data quality scoring, with multi-granularity trajectory+transition sampling, and a formal connection to iw-SFT theory that proves adaptive references strictly dominate static references in tightening the RL objective lower bound.",

This achieves 18x faster training on Clothing-1M by avoiding both noisy and already-learned data. ReLo (Sujit et al., NeurIPS 2023) adapted this principle to RL, computing reducible TD error as the difference between the online network's TD error and the Polyak-averaged (EMA) target network's TD error. Crucially, ReLo's target network is SAC's standard Polyak-averaged target (θ_target ← τ·θ_target + (1-τ)·θ_online, τ≈0.995), which already exists for TD learning stability and serves double duty for reducible loss — ReLo did not introduce an EMA reference, it repurposed an existing RL mechanism. All three works that operate in supervised settings (RHO-LOSS, Rho-1) use static reference models.

Re-Mix (Hejna et al., CoRL 2024, Outstanding Paper Finalist) extends this to robot imitation learning, using excess BC loss relative to a *fixed* reference model with DRO to optimize domain-level weights across heterogeneous robotics datasets (Open X-Embodiment), outperforming uniform weights by 38% and human-selected weights by 32%. Re-Mix operates at *domain level* (one weight per dataset), uses a *fixed* reference model, and employs DRO optimization — not sample-level prioritized sampling.

**Static demonstration curation (one-shot preprocessing):** SCIZOR (ICRA 2026) removes suboptimal and redundant data via self-supervised progress prediction and clustering. CUPID (CoRL 2025) uses influence functions to rank demonstrations by estimated impact on closed-loop performance. QoQ (arXiv 2026) applies static influence-function scoring. RINSE (ICML 2025) proposes smoothness-driven metrics (Spectral Arc Length and Trajectory-Envelope Distance) for policy-architecture-agnostic demonstration scoring.
